scope: What these NASA sources state, put side by side: liquid fuel droplets in microgravity, not cabin materials; a physiological input from NASA documents, not medical guidance.
note: Every value shown by the suit-and-cabin panel is read from an entry below. Quotes are verbatim from the PDF at url; a line break in the PDF is joined with a space (or closed up inside a hyphenated word). Table cells are quoted as one table row. Pages are PDF page numbers. The arithmetic that combines the values is VESTA's, not NASA's.

sources.label: How the ratio R is defined
sources.title: Evidence Report: Risk of Reduced Crew Health and Performance Due to Decompression Sickness and Hypoxia
sources.document: NASA Human Research Program evidence report (2023)
sources.quote: TR is the ratio of computed P1N2 in a theoretical tissue to ambient pressure. Equation 2 defines P1N2, and P2 is the ambient pressure after depressurization.

sources.label: R-value and TR are the same ratio
sources.title: Evidence Report: Risk of Reduced Crew Health and Performance Due to Decompression Sickness and Hypoxia

sources.quote: ratio-value used by NASA, equivalent to P1N2 / P2, also called TR

sources.quote: For example, an R-value of 1.65 or less is acceptable for EVA operations in the 4.3 psia EMU from the Shuttle, but this R-value of 1.65 in an EMU does not mean the P(DCS) is zero

sources.label: Ratio the report pairs with the 5.8 psia suit

sources.quote: Operations using the Russian Orlan spacesuit at 5.8 psia result in an R-value of about 1.85 to provide a P(DCS) equivalent to the P(DCS) in the EMU, so the acceptable R-value (TR) is not an absolute, but in this case it is a function of the suit pressure

sources.label: Why the working group recommended a low-pressure, oxygen-enriched cabin
sources.title: Evidence Report: Risk of Reduced Crew Health and Performance Due to Decompression Sickness and Hypoxia
sources.document: NASA Human Research Program evidence report (2023)
sources.quote: Commissioned in 2005, the Exploration Atmospheres Working Group (EAWG) had the primary goal of recommending internal atmospheres to NASA to enable efficient and repetitive EVAs for missions that were to be enabled by the former Constellation Program. At the conclusion of the EAWG meeting, the 8.0 psia and 32% oxygen (O2) environment was recommended for EVA-intensive phases of exploration missions.

sources.label: Reasons the 2015 report gives for that choice
sources.title: Evidence Report: Risk of Hypobaric Hypoxia from the Exploration Atmosphere
sources.document: NASA Human Research Program evidence report (2015)
sources.quote: The 8 psia / 32% O2 (henceforth referred to as 8/32) environment was selected because it was considered to be a mildly hypoxic atmosphere with acceptable flammability risk and low O2 prebreathe (PB) overhead to maintain acceptable DCS risk [1].

sources.label: Exploration atmosphere, 2023 report
sources.title: Evidence Report: Risk of Reduced Crew Health and Performance Due to Decompression Sickness and Hypoxia
sources.document: NASA Human Research Program evidence report (2023)
sources.quote: After re-evaluation in 2012, the 8.0 psia/32% O2 environment was altered to 8.2 psia and 34% O2 to reduce the hypoxic stress of a crewmember through increasing alveolar O2 pressure by 11 mmHg

sources.label: Exploration atmosphere, 2026 memorandum quoting HEO-DM-1006
sources.title: Impacts of Reduced Pressure Atmospheres on Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) Architectures
sources.quote: HEO-DM-1006 [ref. 15] specifies that a nominal total cabin pressure of 8.2 psia and O2 greater than or equal to 33.7% is needed for Exploration missions with high-frequency EVA.
